rules.title: AB 325 Cartwright Act: violations (Common pricing algorithms)
rules.requirement: It is unlawful to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, combination or conspiracy to restrain trade, or to use or distribute one while coercing another person to adopt its recommended price or commercial term. A common pricing algorithm is any methodology used by two or more persons that uses competitor data to recommend, align, stabilize, set or influence a price or commercial term. Complaints need only plausibly allege a contract, combination or conspiracy.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to any person using or distributing a common pricing algorithm, across all products and services, not only housing.
rules.exemptions: The term 'person' does not include the end consumer of a product or service.
rules.citation: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16729 (added by AB 325, Stats. 2025, ch. 338)
rules.quoted_span: It shall be unlawful for a person to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, combination in the form of a trust, or conspiracy to restrain trade or commerce in violation of this chapter.

rules.title: Berkeley Municipal Code Chapter 13.63 (Ordinance No. 7,992-N.S.): Prohibition on the Sale or Use of Coordinated Pricing Algorithms to Set Rents or Manage Occupancy Levels for Residential Dwelling Units
rules.requirement: It is unlawful to sell, license or provide to Berkeley landlords a coordinated pricing algorithm that sets or recommends rents or occupancy levels, and unlawful for landlords to use one. Each month of violation and each dwelling unit is a separate violation.
rules.key_value: Civil penalties up to $1,000 per violation
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to coordinated pricing algorithms using non-public Competitor Data less than 90 days old to set or recommend rents or occupancy for Berkeley residential units.
rules.exemptions: Excludes aggregated anonymous reports, affordable-housing rent or income limit tools, and market research, appraisal or software development uses.
rules.citation: Berkeley Municipal Code Chapter 13.63; Ordinance No. 7,992-N.S.
rules.quoted_span:
It shall be unlawful to sell, license, or otherwise provide to City of Berkeley 
landlords any coordinated pricing algorithm that sets or recommends rents or occupancy 
levels that may be achieved for residential dwelling units in the City of Berkeley.

rules.title: Berkeley Rent Ordinance security deposit interest
rules.requirement: Landlords of units fully or partially covered by the Rent Ordinance must pay tenants interest on security deposits at the end of each year, and a prorated amount if the tenant moves out before year end.
rules.key_value: Annual interest on deposits
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to tenancies in units fully or partially covered by the Berkeley Rent Ordinance.
rules.quoted_span: For tenancies in units fully or partially covered by Berkeley's Rent Ordinance, landlords must pay tenants interest on their security deposit at the end of each year and a prorated amount if the tenant moves out before the end of the year.

rules.title: Ellis Implementation Ordinance
rules.requirement: Owners who evict tenants to remove a property from the rental market must pay the same relocation assistance as for owner move-in evictions. The payment is indexed to inflation; for 2026 the standard payment is $19,413 and the additional payment for qualifying households is $6,471.
rules.key_value: $19,413 standard relocation payment; $6,471 additional for qualifying households (effective 2026-01-01)
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to Ellis Act evictions removing a property from the rental market.
rules.interaction: A state rule of this category yields to this local rule.
rules.quoted_span: The Ellis Implementation Ordinance requires the same relocation assistance payments for tenants evicted so the owner can remove a property from the rental housing market.

rules.title: Berkeley Rent Stabilization and Eviction for Just Cause Ordinance
rules.requirement: Just cause for eviction applies to fully covered and partially covered units. Only the exempt categories (golden duplex, owner-shared kitchen or bath, owner-occupied ADU properties, university housing, nonprofit cooperatives) are outside it.
rules.coverage_conditions: Just cause protections cover all fully and partially covered units, including newer construction, condos and post-1995 single-family tenancies.
rules.exemptions: Golden duplexes, owner-shared kitchen/bath units, owner-occupied ADU properties, university housing and nonprofit cooperatives are exempt.
rules.interaction: A state rule of this category yields to this local rule.
rules.citation: Berkeley Rent Stabilization and Eviction for Just Cause Ordinance
rules.quoted_span:
New construction: units that were built and received a Certificate of 
Occupancy after June 1980** 
Partially Covered Yes No Yes Yes

rules.title: Berkeley Municipal Code Chapter 13.78 (Tenant Screening and Application Fees)
rules.requirement: Owners who charge a screening fee must give a clear and conspicuous Tenant Screening Fee Rights Statement and state the maximum fee cap under Civil Code 1950.6(b) before receiving the fee. Owners may not charge existing tenants a non-refundable fee for renewing a tenancy or for adding, replacing or removing a roommate. The chapter applies to all residential rental agreements, and any contrary lease provision is unenforceable.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to all residential rental agreements in Berkeley regardless of contrary lease language.
rules.quoted_span: An owner of residential rental property (or the owner’s agent) cannot charge a non-refundable fee to any existing tenant for the purpose of renewing a tenancy, in whole or in part, including any fee associated with the departure of a roommate or to request to add or replace a roommate in a pre-existing household.

rules.title: Berkeley Rent Stabilization and Eviction for Just Cause Ordinance
rules.requirement: Rent control applies only to fully covered units: most pre-1980 multifamily units, single-family homes with tenancies that began before 1996, and rooming houses. Newer construction, post-1995 single-family tenancies, most condominiums, certain subsidized units and several owner-related or institutional units are not rent controlled.
rules.coverage_conditions: Fully covered units (most pre-1980 multifamily, pre-1996 single-family tenancies, rooming houses) are subject to rent control.
rules.exemptions: Partially covered units (post-June 1980 construction, post-1995 single-family tenancies, most condos, certain subsidized units) and exempt units (golden duplex, shared kitchen/bath, owner-occupied ADU properties, dormitories, nonprofit cooperatives) have no rent control.
rules.citation: Berkeley Rent Stabilization and Eviction for Just Cause Ordinance
rules.quoted_span: Most units in multifamily properties built before 1980** Fully Covered Yes Yes Yes Yes

rules.title: Ronald V. Dellums Fair Chance Access to Housing Ordinance
rules.requirement: Rental housing providers may not ask about or use criminal history in advertising, applications, tenant selection or tenancy decisions, including refusing to rent, demanding higher deposits or rent, or disqualifying people from rental assistance. Before taking any adverse action based on criminal history, the landlord must give written notice and an opportunity to respond.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to rental housing providers in Berkeley with respect to current and prospective tenants.
rules.exemptions: Exempts lifetime sex offenders, limited public housing/Section 8 cases, owner-occupied 1-3 unit properties, owner move-back rental agreements, and existing tenants subletting or adding roommates.
rules.quoted_span: The Fair Chance Access to Housing Ordinance prohibits rental housing providers in Berkeley from asking about and using criminal history and/or criminal background checks in their rental housing advertising, applications, tenant selection process, or decision-making.

rules.title: California Civil Code section 1950.5 (Security deposits for residential rental property)
rules.requirement: A landlord may not demand or receive security above one month's rent (two months' rent for small natural-person landlords owning no more than two properties with four units in total, unless the tenant is a service member). The landlord must do an initial inspection on request, take photographs, and send an itemized statement and any remaining deposit within 21 calendar days after the tenant vacates.
rules.key_value: Maximum security of one month's rent (two months for small landlords); return within 21 calendar days
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to security for rental agreements for residential property used as the tenant's dwelling.
rules.exemptions: The two-month cap applies only to landlords who are natural persons (or LLCs of natural persons) with no more than two properties and four units. It does not apply to service-member tenants. An advance payment of six months' rent or more is allowed for leases of six months or longer.
rules.quoted_span: (1) Except as provided in paragraph (2), (3), or (5), a landlord shall not demand or receive security, however denominated, in an amount or value in excess of an amount equal to one month’s rent, in addition to any rent for the first month paid on or before initial occupancy.

rules.title: California Civil Code section 1946.2 (Tenant Protection Act of 2019 – just cause)
rules.requirement: After a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied a unit for 12 months, the owner may not terminate the tenancy without stating a just cause (at-fault or no-fault) in the written notice. For no-fault terminations the owner must pay one month's rent as relocation assistance (within 15 days of notice) or waive the final month's rent.
rules.key_value: 12 months occupancy; relocation assistance equal to one month's rent
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to residential tenancies of 12 months or more (24 months if adult tenants were added to the lease) statewide.
rules.exemptions: Exempts recently built housing (certificate of occupancy within 15 years), hotels, institutional housing, owner-shared or owner-occupied small properties, qualifying non-corporate-owned single-unit properties, affordable housing, and properties covered by local just cause ordinances.
rules.interaction: Yields to a stricter local rule where one applies.
rules.quoted_span: (a) Notwithstanding any other law, after a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied a residential real property for 12 months, the owner of the residential real property shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause, which shall be stated in the written notice to terminate tenancy.

rules.title: California Civil Code section 1950.6 (Application Screening Fees)
rules.requirement: Landlords may charge an application screening fee only up to actual out-of-pocket costs and the reasonable value of time, capped at $30 per applicant (CPI-adjustable). No fee may be charged if no unit is or will soon be available; the landlord must offer first-come processing or refund unselected applicants, provide an itemized receipt, return unused amounts, and give the applicant a copy of the credit report.
rules.key_value: $30 per applicant, adjustable annually by CPI from January 1, 1998
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to owners of residential rental property and their agents who charge application screening fees to rental applicants and guarantors.
rules.exemptions: The section does not preempt rules on deposits and fees under federal or state housing assistance programs.
rules.quoted_span: In no case shall the amount of the application screening fee charged by the landlord or their agent be greater than thirty dollars ($30) per applicant. The thirty dollar ($30) application screening fee may be adjusted annually by the landlord or their agent commensurate with an increase in the Consumer Price Index, beginning on January 1, 1998.

rules.title: Just Cause For Eviction Ordinance (JCO)
rules.requirement: Landlords may not terminate covered tenancies without just cause (at-fault reasons or specified no-fault reasons). No-fault evictions require relocation assistance; evictions for non-payment require the amount owed to exceed Fair Market Rent; eviction notices must be filed with LAHD within three business days.
rules.key_value: Relocation assistance for no-fault evictions; rent owed must exceed FMR for non-payment eviction
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to most Los Angeles residential rentals not covered by the RSO after six months of tenancy or expiry of the original lease.
rules.exemptions: Exceptions include transient hotels, licensed care facilities, fraternity or sorority houses, owner's roommate, certain cooperatives, some homeless or treatment facilities and some government-owned properties.
rules.interaction: A state rule of this category yields to this local rule.
rules.quoted_span: It prohibits terminations of tenancies without just cause and requires relocation assistance for no-fault evictions.

rules.title: Resident Protections Ordinance (RPO) relocation for demolition for new construction
rules.requirement: Landlords terminating tenancies of Protected Units to demolish for new construction must file with LAHD, serve notice, and pay relocation under the state Housing Crisis Act or city law, whichever is higher; lower income households receive enhanced standardized payments. Occupant protections include a right to remain up to 6 months, right to return and right of first refusal.
rules.key_value: Standardized payment: $115,480 extremely low, $96,750 very low, $87,450 low income (effective July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2027)
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to Protected Units (including all RSO units) demolished for new construction.
rules.interaction: A state rule of this category yields to this local rule.
rules.quoted_span:
Failure to comply with the RPO may result in 
financial penalties starting at $250,000 per displaced unit and withholding of LAHD permit clearances.

rules.title: Rent Stabilization Ordinance (RSO)
rules.requirement: Rent for covered units may be increased only once every 12 months by the allowable percentage set by the city. Certain additional surcharges and LAHD-approved increases (capital improvements, primary renovation, seismic retrofit, rehabilitation, just and reasonable) are allowed, and rent may go to market rate after specified vacancies.
rules.key_value: Once every 12 months by the allowable rent increase percentage; no utility add-on from 2026-02-02
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to rental properties first built on or before October 1, 1978 (apartments, duplexes, ADUs, mobile homes and similar), plus replacement units.
rules.exemptions: Condos and townhomes with tenancies commencing after December 31, 1995 are not rent-regulated; a luxury exemption may be sought.

rules.title: California Civil Code section 1947.12 (Tenant Protection Act rent cap, as amended by SB 567)
rules.requirement: An owner of residential real property may not increase the gross rental rate over any 12-month period by more than 5 percent plus the local percentage change in cost of living, or 10 percent, whichever is lower. No more than two increments are allowed in 12 months, and the initial rent for a new tenancy is not capped.
rules.key_value: 5% plus CPI change, capped at 10% per 12 months
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to residential dwellings and units in California, including mobilehome park units, for rent increases on or after March 15, 2019 (February 18, 2021 for mobilehome tenancies).
rules.exemptions: Exempts deed-restricted or subsidized affordable housing, dormitories, housing under stricter local rent control, housing with a certificate of occupancy within the past 15 years, certain separately alienable properties with non-corporate owners, owner-occupied duplexes, and mobilehome homeowners.
rules.quoted_span: Subject to subdivision (b), an owner of residential real property shall not, over the course of any 12-month period, increase the gross rental rate for a dwelling or a unit more than 5 percent plus the percentage change in the cost of living, or 10 percent, whichever is lower, of the lowest gross rental rate charged for that dwelling or unit at any time during the 12 months prior to the effective date of the increase.

rules.title: Prohibition of Anti-Competitive Automated Rent Price-Fixing Ordinance (San Diego Municipal Code Chapter 9, Article 8, Division 11)
rules.requirement: Bans selling, licensing or providing algorithmic devices that use nonpublic competitor data to recommend rents or occupancy levels to landlords, and bans landlords from using them to set rents or occupancy for residential rental property. Tenants may sue for injunctive relief, damages or civil penalties.
rules.key_value: Civil penalties up to $1,000 per violation; each month and each property is a separate violation
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to sellers of algorithmic devices and landlords using them for residential rental property in San Diego.
rules.exemptions: Excludes aggregated reports from public or 90-day-old historical data and software used to set rents or income limits under affordable housing program guidelines.
rules.quoted_span:
It is unlawful for a person to sell, license, or otherwise provide an
algorithmic device to a landlord.
(b) It is unlawful for a landlord to use an algorithmic device to set rental rates
or occupancy levels for residential rental property.

rules.title: San Diego Municipal Code Chapter 9, Article 8, Division 7: Residential Tenant Protections (Tenants' Right to Know Regulations)
rules.requirement: A landlord may not terminate a tenancy without just cause, either at-fault (e.g. non-payment, breach, nuisance) or no-fault (owner move-in, withdrawal from market, government order, demolition or substantial remodel). No-fault terminations carry notice content, re-offer and relocation duties, and landlords must give tenants a written notice of protections with the Tenant Protection Guide.
rules.key_value: Owner move-in requires occupancy within 90 days for at least 12 continuous months; substantial remodel requires vacating at least 30 continuous days
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to residential rental tenancies of more than 30 days in San Diego.
rules.exemptions: Exempts transient, affordable/subsidized, mobilehome, institutional, some owner-occupied, buildings with a certificate of occupancy within 15 years, and qualifying separately alienable properties with non-corporate landlords.
rules.interaction: A state rule of this category yields to this local rule.
rules.quoted_span:
A landlord shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause. For purposes of this 
Division, just cause includes at-fault just cause and no-fault just cause.

rules.title: Section 37.10C of the San Francisco Rent Ordinance
rules.requirement: Prohibits the sale or use of algorithmic devices to set rents or manage occupancy levels for residential units in San Francisco. A tenant or the City Attorney may bring a civil action over violations.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to algorithmic devices used to set rents or manage occupancy for residential units in San Francisco.
rules.quoted_span: The law prohibits the sale or use of such algorithmic devices and allows a tenant or the City Attorney to bring a civil action if they believe an entity is in violation of the law.

rules.title: San Francisco Security Deposit Interest Rate
rules.requirement: Landlords must pay interest on security deposits at the rate set annually by the Rent Board. For March 1, 2026 – February 28, 2027 the rate is 4.2%.
rules.key_value: 4.2% for March 1, 2026 – February 28, 2027
rules.citation: Rent Board Security Deposit Interest Rates
rules.quoted_span:
Security Deposit Interest:
4.2% for March 1, 2026 – February 28, 2027

rules.title: San Francisco Rent Ordinance Section 37.9(a) – Just Cause Evictions
rules.requirement: A landlord of a unit covered by the Rent Ordinance may evict only for a listed "just cause" reason that is the dominant motive for the eviction. Expiration of a rental agreement or a change in ownership is not just cause; removing housing services also needs just cause.
rules.key_value: 17 just cause reasons
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to rental units covered by the San Francisco Rent Ordinance, including some units exempt from its rent increase limits (post-June 13, 1979 Certificate of Occupancy units, Costa-Hawkins-eligible tenancies, and some other government-regulated tenancies).
rules.interaction: A state rule of this category yields to this local rule.
rules.quoted_span: In order to evict a tenant from a rental unit covered by the Rent Ordinance, a landlord must have a "just cause" reason that is the dominant motive for pursuing the eviction.

rules.title: San Francisco Rent Ordinance – Allowable Annual Rent Increase
rules.requirement: The Rent Board sets the allowable annual rent increase for rent-controlled units each March 1 – February 28 period. For March 1, 2026 – February 28, 2027 the allowed increase is 1.6%.
rules.key_value: 1.6% for March 1, 2026 – February 28, 2027
rules.citation: Rent Ordinance (Rent Board allowable annual increases)
rules.quoted_span:
Allowable Rent Increase:
1.6% for March 1, 2026 – February 28, 2027

rules.title: Santa Ana algorithmic rent-setting software ordinance
rules.requirement: Prohibits the sale, licensing, provision and use of certain algorithmic rent-setting software for residential rental property in Santa Ana. Tenants may sue directly and need only prove the landlord used the prohibited technology, not intentional collusion.
rules.key_value: Civil penalties up to $1,000 per violation
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to residential rental property within Santa Ana city limits.
rules.exemptions: Does not apply to pricing software relying solely on public or aggregate historical data, or tools used to comply with affordable housing programs.
rules.citation: Santa Ana algorithmic rent-setting software ordinance (no number given)
rules.quoted_span: The ordinance, approved on Tuesday, Feb. 17, for a first reading and set for a final vote on March 3, prohibits the sale, licensing, provision and use of certain algorithmic rent-setting software for residential rental properties.

rules.title: Just Cause Eviction Ordinance
rules.requirement: After 30 days, an owner may not terminate a tenancy without just cause stated in a written notice, and must first give notice and a chance to cure. For no-fault terminations the owner must provide 3 months of relocation assistance or waive the final 3 months of rent.
rules.key_value: 3 months relocation assistance or rent waiver for no-fault terminations
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to residential tenancies in Santa Ana after 30 days of tenancy.
rules.exemptions: Exempts housing produced in the last 15 years, deed-restricted affordable housing, hotels/transient occupancy, hospital and care facilities, dormitories and other shared living quarters.
rules.interaction: A state rule of this category yields to this local rule.
rules.citation: Santa Ana Just Cause Eviction Ordinance
rules.quoted_span: After 30 days, an owner shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause, which shall be stated in a written notice.

rules.title: Rent Stabilization Ordinance
rules.requirement: Residential rent increases are limited to the lower of 3% per year or 80% of the CPI change over the most recent 12 months; no increase if CPI is negative. Owners may petition for relief and must give written notice of the ordinance and tenant rights.
rules.key_value: Lower of 3% per year or 80% of CPI change
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to residential rental units and mobile home spaces in Santa Ana.
rules.exemptions: Buildings constructed after February 1, 1995 and mobile home spaces offered for rent after January 1, 1990 are exempt.
rules.quoted_span: Increase in residential rents are limited to the lower of 3% per year, or 80% of the percent change in the Consumer Price Index over the most recent 12-month period. If the CPI is negative, no rent increase is permitted.

rules.title: California Government Code section 12955 (Fair Employment and Housing Act, housing discrimination; source of income)
rules.requirement: Housing providers may not discriminate against applicants based on source of income, which includes government subsidies such as Section 8 and HUD-VASH vouchers. Where a government rent subsidy applies, income standards must be based on the tenant's portion of the rent, and applicants must be allowed to offer alternative evidence of ability to pay instead of credit history.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to owners of housing accommodations and others in housing transactions, with the subsidy-specific income and credit rules applying where a government rent subsidy exists.
rules.exemptions: Inquiring about the level or source of income is not source-of-income discrimination, and owners may verify employment, request landlord references or verify identity.
rules.quoted_span: (o) (1) In instances in which there is a government rent subsidy, to do either of the following:

rules.title: An Act relative to preventing algorithmic rent fixing in the rental housing market
rules.requirement: Bill H.5222 is aimed at preventing algorithmic rent fixing in the rental housing market. The chunk gives only the title and status, with no operative text, definitions or penalties.
rules.quoted_span: An Act relative to preventing algorithmic rent fixing in the rental housing market

rules.title: An Act prohibiting algorithmic rent setting
rules.requirement: Bill S.2983 would prohibit algorithmic rent setting in Massachusetts. The chunk shows only the title and history, not the bill's text, so definitions and prohibited conduct are not stated.
rules.quoted_span: An Act prohibiting algorithmic rent setting

rules.title: Housing Stability Notification Act
rules.requirement: Landlords and foreclosing owners who intend to end a tenancy or post-foreclosure occupancy must give the tenant a Notice of Tenants' Rights and Resources at the same time as the Notice to Quit or notice of lease non-renewal. They must also send a copy of that notice, with a Certificate of Compliance/Service, to the City's Office of Housing Stability. The requirements cannot be waived.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to all landlords and foreclosing owners intending to end a tenancy or post-foreclosure occupancy of a unit in Boston.
rules.exemptions: Residences in hospitals, skilled nursing or health facilities, and in non-profit short-term substance abuse treatment facilities are exempt.
rules.quoted_span:
The Notice of
Tenants’ Rights and Resources must be delivered at the same time as the Notice to
Quit.

rules.title: Boston Fair Housing Regulations
rules.requirement: It is illegal in Boston to discriminate in renting, buying, selling or financing housing based on rental assistance, such as Section 8 vouchers. A landlord who says they do not accept rental assistance (Section 8, social security disability or veterans vouchers) is engaging in housing discrimination.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to renting, buying, selling or financing housing in the City of Boston.
rules.quoted_span:
The landlord tells you they don't accept rental assistance. This includes Section
8 vouchers, social security disability vouchers, and veterans vouchers.

rules.title: Boston Fair Chance Tenant Selection Policy
rules.requirement: Housing providers with DND funding or land, or BPDA inclusionary income-restricted units, may not use blanket bans based on arrests or convictions and must review applicants case by case. They may not consider non-conviction arrests, convictions with judicial relief, juvenile records, or convictions over 5 years old, and may not use credit scores to approve or deny applications.
rules.key_value: Convictions more than 5 years old may not be considered
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to housing providers with DND funding or land, or BPDA inclusionary income-restricted units.
rules.exemptions: The arrest and conviction limits do not apply where a conviction directly relates to the housing or poses unreasonable risk to others' safety, or to current criminal behavior. Conflicting federal or state law also preempts the policy.
rules.citation: Boston Fair Chance Tenant Selection Policy (DND, February 2017)
rules.quoted_span:
Housing providers receiving Department of Neighborhood Development (DND) funding and/or 
land, or that have income restricted units created under the Boston Planning and Development 
Agency (BPDA) Inclusionary Development Policy will not impose a blanket policy that denies 
housing to anyone with arrests and or convictions. Housing providers will consider applicants on 
a case-by-case basis.

rules.title: City Council policy order on algorithmic rent pricing
rules.requirement: The City Council unanimously passed a policy order starting steps to ban residential property management companies from contracting with firms that use algorithmic or AI-driven models to recommend rents. The city manager is directed to work with city departments to draft policy options or ordinance language and present them to the council later this term.
rules.coverage_conditions: Would apply to residential property management companies that contract with algorithmic rent-recommendation firms.
rules.citation: City Council policy order (June 2026), no number given
rules.quoted_span: City council also unanimously passed a policy order initiating steps to ban residential property management companies from contracting companies that use algorithmic and AI-driven models to recommend what they should charge for rent.

rules.title: Cambridge Fair Housing Ordinance, chapter 14.04
rules.requirement: Landlords, sellers and rental agents may not discriminate in renting, including on the basis of source of income (which includes Section 8 and public benefits). They may use any reasonable tenant-selection standard, such as ability to pay rent and ability to care for the apartment, if it is applied equally and uniformly to all applicants.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to housing rentals, sales and related real estate transactions in Cambridge.
rules.exemptions: Two-family dwellings where the owner lives are exempt.
rules.quoted_span: Under the law, landlords, sellers and rental agents may use any reasonable standard to determine which applicants are selected, as long as that standard is applied equally and uniformly to all applicants.

rules.title: M.G.L. c. 186, § 15B (Security deposits; prepaid rent)
rules.requirement: A lessor may not collect more than first month's rent, last month's rent, a security deposit of one month's rent, and the cost of a key and lock. Deposits must be held in a separate interest-bearing Massachusetts bank account, with a receipt and statement of condition, 5% annual interest (or the lesser bank rate), and return within 30 days of tenancy end less itemized permitted deductions.
rules.key_value: Security deposit capped at 1 month's rent; 5% annual interest; return within 30 days
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to lessors and their agents of residential real property in Massachusetts.
rules.quoted_span: (iii) a security deposit equal to the first month's rent provided that such security deposit is deposited as required by subsection (3) and that the tenant is given the statement of condition as required by subsection (2)

rules.title: Determination of lease for nonpayment of rent
rules.requirement: For nonpayment of rent under a written lease, the landlord must give the tenant 14 days' written notice to quit. The tenant can stop the termination by paying all rent due, with interest and costs, on or before the answer day in a possession action. If nonpayment was caused by a government delay in delivering a rental or subsistence payment, the court must continue the hearing at least seven days and treat the tenancy as not terminated if full payment is tendered in that time.
rules.key_value: 14 days' written notice to quit
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to tenancies under a written lease where rent is unpaid.
rules.quoted_span: Upon the neglect or refusal to pay the rent due under a written lease, fourteen days' notice to quit, given in writing by the landlord to the tenant, shall be sufficient to determine the lease, unless the tenant, on or before the day the answer is due, in an action by the landlord to recover possession of the premises, pays or tenders to the landlord or to his attorney all rent then due, with interest and costs of suit.

rules.title: An Act petition for a special law authorizing the city of Boston to implement rent stabilization and tenant eviction protections (H.3744)
rules.requirement: Home-rule petition that would authorize the city of Boston to implement tenant eviction protections. The page gives no operative text, so the grounds, notice and relocation duties are not stated.
rules.coverage_conditions: Would apply only in the city of Boston if enacted and implemented.
rules.quoted_span: An Act petition for a special law authorizing the city of Boston to implement rent stabilization and tenant eviction protections

rules.title: Notice to quit for nonpayment of rent
rules.requirement: A written notice to quit for nonpayment of rent given to a residential tenant must be accompanied by a state-developed form with documentation of repayment agreements, information on rental assistance, court rules and legal eviction restrictions, and a prominent statement that the notice is not an eviction. Courts may not accept a summary process filing for nonpayment without proof the form was delivered.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to written notices to quit for nonpayment of rent given to residential tenants.
rules.quoted_span: No court having jurisdiction over an action for summary process pursuant to chapter 239, including the Boston municipal court department, shall, in an eviction for nonpayment of rent for a residential dwelling unit, accept for filing a writ, summons or complaint without proof of delivery of the form required under this section.

rules.title: Reprisal for reporting violations of law or for tenant's union activity (G.L. c. 186, § 18)
rules.requirement: Landlords and their agents may not threaten or take reprisals against a residential tenant for enforcing housing laws, reporting code violations, or organizing or joining a tenants' union. A termination of tenancy (other than for nonpayment), rent increase or substantial change in tenancy terms within six months of such activity is presumed to be a reprisal, and the landlord can rebut this only by clear and convincing evidence.
rules.key_value: Six-month rebuttable presumption; damages of one to three months' rent or actual damages, whichever is greater
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to tenants of residential premises who engage in protected activity such as reporting violations, enforcing housing laws or organizing a tenants' union.
rules.exemptions: Notices of termination for nonpayment of rent do not trigger the presumption.
rules.quoted_span: The receipt of any notice of termination of tenancy, except for nonpayment of rent, or, of increase in rent, or, of any substantial alteration in the terms of tenancy within six months after the tenant has commenced, proceeded with, or obtained relief in such action, exercised such rights, made such report or complaint, or organized or joined such tenants' union or within six months after any other person has taken such action or actions on behalf of the tenant or in, or relating to, the building in which the tenant resides, shall create a rebuttable presumption that such notice or other action is a reprisal against the tenant for engaging in such activities.

rules.title: 254 CMR 7 (broker regulations on fees to prospective tenants)
rules.requirement: Licensed brokers may charge fees to prospective tenants if they follow the board of registration's rules. The broker must give the applicant written notice of the fee amount, the time and manner of payment, and whether the fee is contingent on a lease. The applicant signs the notice, and any refusal is recorded, at the first personal meeting.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to licensed brokers finding dwellings for prospective tenants for a fee.
rules.quoted_span: In addition to holding a valid license, the broker has to tell the applicant in writing the amount of the broker’s fee, the time and manner of payment, and whether it is contingent on the owner and applicant actually entering into a lease or rental agreement.

rules.title: M.G.L. c. 186, § 15B (limits on upfront charges by lessors)
rules.requirement: Before a tenancy begins, a lessor may require payment only of first month's rent, last month's rent, a security deposit and a lock-change fee. Application, screening, pet, cleaning and amenity fees are forbidden for landlords.
rules.key_value: Only first, last, security deposit and locks
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to lessors (landlords) collecting payments before a tenancy begins.
rules.exemptions: Licensed brokers may charge fees under the board of registration regulations (254 CMR 7).
rules.quoted_span: It states that prior to the beginning of a tenancy, no lessor may require payment for anything except first, last, security, and locks ( MGL Ch 186 Section 15B ).

rules.title: Real estate brokers and salesmen; persons finding dwelling accommodations for fee
rules.requirement: Only licensed brokers or salespersons may find dwelling accommodations for prospective tenants for a fee. From August 1, 2025, a broker may contract solely with either the tenant or the landlord, and any fee may be paid only by the party who originally engaged and contracted with the broker.
rules.key_value: Fee payable only by the party (landlord or tenant) who engaged the broker
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to persons finding dwelling accommodations for prospective tenants for a fee.
rules.quoted_span: Any fee shall only be paid by the party, lessor or tenant who originally engaged and entered into a contract with the licensed broker or salesperson.

rules.title: An Act petition for a special law authorizing the city of Boston to implement rent stabilization and tenant eviction protections (H.3744)
rules.requirement: Home-rule petition that would authorize the city of Boston to implement rent stabilization. The page gives no operative text, so no cap or formula is stated.
rules.coverage_conditions: Would apply only in the city of Boston if enacted and implemented.
rules.quoted_span: An Act petition for a special law authorizing the city of Boston to implement rent stabilization and tenant eviction protections

rules.title: General Laws Chapter 40P, Section 4: General prohibition; exception
rules.requirement: No city or town may enact, maintain or enforce rent control of any kind. A municipality that accepts the chapter may adopt only voluntary rent control that excludes regulation of occupancy, services, evictions and condominium conversion, and it must compensate owners from general funds for the difference between fair market rent and the controlled rent.
rules.key_value: Rent control barred; exception limited to voluntary regulation of owners with ten or more units and fair market rent of $400 or less
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to all cities and towns in Massachusetts, with a narrow exception for municipalities that accept chapter 40P.
rules.exemptions: Accepting municipalities may adopt voluntary rent control, which cannot apply to units owned by a person or entity owning fewer than ten rental units or to units with fair market rent above $400.
rules.quoted_span: No city or town may enact, maintain or enforce rent control of any kind, except that any city or town that accepts this chapter may adopt rent control regulation that provides:

rules.title: Initiative Petition 25-21, An Initiative Petition to Protect Tenants by Limiting Rent Increases
rules.requirement: Would have repealed the state ban on rent control and capped annual rent increases statewide on most residential rental units. The SJC in Cella v. Attorney General held it cannot appear on the November 2026 ballot because its religious-facility exemption relates to religion.
rules.key_value: Lesser of annual CPI increase or 5% per year
rules.coverage_conditions: Would have applied to most residential rental units statewide.
rules.exemptions: Exempts owner-occupied buildings of four or fewer units, units under 10 years old, certain publicly regulated units, short-term rentals, and facilities operated solely for educational, religious or nonprofit purposes.
rules.citation: Initiative Petition 25-21; Cella v. Attorney General, SJC-13893
rules.quoted_span: Under the proposed law, annual rent increases would have been limited to the lesser of the annual increase in the Consumer Price Index or 5%.

rules.title: Massachusetts Fair Housing Act (G.L. c. 151B, § 4(10)) – public assistance and housing subsidy discrimination
rules.requirement: It is unlawful for anyone furnishing rental accommodations to discriminate against an individual because they receive public assistance or a housing subsidy, including rental assistance, or because of any requirement of such a program.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to any person furnishing credit, services or rental accommodations to recipients of public assistance or housing subsidies.
rules.quoted_span: For any person furnishing credit, services or rental accommodations to discriminate against any individual who is a recipient of federal, state, or local public assistance, including medical assistance, or who is a tenant receiving federal, state, or local housing subsidies, including rental assistance or rental supplements, because the individual is such a recipient, or because of any requirement of such public assistance, rental assistance, or housing subsidy program.

rules.title: Forbidding the Algorithmic Inflation of Rent (FAIR) Act
rules.requirement: Makes it an antitrust violation for rental property owners to pay for or use a coordinator's services, for anyone to perform a coordinating function (algorithmic setting or recommending of rents, lease terms or occupancy using shared competitively sensitive information), or to engage in or facilitate parallel pricing coordination. Government affordability controls, public free rent estimates, research use and equal-terms brokerage databases are excluded.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to rental property owners, coordinators and other persons dealing with rental residential dwelling units in New Jersey.
rules.exemptions: Excludes government entities setting rents via affordability controls and certain research, public estimate and brokerage database uses.
rules.quoted_span:
It
shall be unlawful and a violation of the “New Jersey Antitrust Act,” P.L.1970,
c.73 (C.56:9-1 et seq.) for:
a.     a rental property owner, or any agent,
representative, or subcontractor thereof, to receive, subscribe to, contract
for, or otherwise exchange any form of consideration in return for the use of,
the services of a coordinator;

rules.title: New Jersey Security Deposit Law
rules.requirement: Landlords may collect a security deposit of no more than one and one-half times one month's rent, and annual increases may not exceed 10% of the current deposit. Deposits must be held in trust in an interest-bearing account, interest belongs to the tenant, and the tenant must receive written notice of the bank and account details within 30 days.
rules.key_value: 1.5 times one month's rent; annual increase up to 10%
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to most residential rental properties, including mobile homes.
rules.exemptions: Owner-occupied two- or three-family dwellings are exempt unless the tenant requests coverage in writing, and the interest-account provisions do not apply to seasonal rentals.
rules.quoted_span:
The maximum-security deposit to be collected by the landlord cannot be more than 
one and one-half times one month’s rent ( N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.2 ). It can be less. Any additional 
yearly security deposit increase may not exceed 10% of the current security deposit.

rules.title: Anti-Eviction Act
rules.requirement: A landlord may recover possession of a residential unit only by consent or through court eviction, and must have good cause to evict or fail to renew a lease. Each cause except nonpayment must be described in a written Notice to Quit (and sometimes a Notice to Cease), and a Judgment for Possession must be entered before the tenant must move.
rules.key_value: Warrant for possession not issuable until 3 business days after judgment; tenant then has 3 business days to move
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to most residential rentals including houses, mobile homes, apartments and rooming/boarding homes.
rules.exemptions: Does not apply to certain small owner-occupied premises, transient or seasonal hotel/motel guests, and units held in trust for a developmentally disabled family member.
rules.quoted_span:
No residential landlord may evict or fail to renew a 
lease, whether it is a written or an oral lease without good cause.

rules.title: P.L. 2025, c.405 (Residential rental property application fee limit)
rules.requirement: A landlord or agent may not require an application or similar fee to apply to lease or sublease a residential rental property that exceeds $50. The cap is adjusted each January 1 by the percent change in the regional CPI, only when that change is above zero.
rules.key_value: $50 cap, adjusted annually for CPI
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to application fees for residential rental property leased or subleased for dwelling purposes.
rules.exemptions: Does not apply to units in one- or two-family dwellings or to NJ Real Estate Commission licensees who are not the landlord.
rules.quoted_span:
A landlord, or
agent thereof, shall not require an application or other similar fee to apply
to lease or sublease a residential rental property for dwelling purposes, which
exceeds $50.

rules.title: Rent Control Ordinance, Chapter 260 of the Jersey City Municipal Code
rules.requirement: Jersey City administers and enforces a rent control ordinance regulating rent increases, with landlord applications for capital improvement, vacancy and hardship increases and tenant petitions for illegal rent or failure to maintain services. All 1-4 unit properties are exempt from rent control.
rules.exemptions: Properties with 1-4 units are exempt, and the ordinance allows other permitted exemptions by owner request.
rules.citation: Chapter 260 of the Jersey City Municipal Code
rules.quoted_span:
The Office of Landlord Tenant Relations administers and enforces the
Rent Control Ordinance, Chapter 260
of the Jersey City Municipal Code and provides education, information and referrals to city residents in connection with landlord/tenant issues.

rules.title: Rent Control/Rent Increases in New Jersey (Anti-Eviction Act notice and unconscionability standard; Newly Constructed Multiple Dwellings Law)
rules.requirement: The State sets no rent control. Municipalities may adopt rent control ordinances, and a landlord may raise rent only by terminating the lease and giving proper written notice. The increase must not be unconscionable and must comply with local ordinances. Newly constructed multiple dwellings are exempt from local rent control for 30 years, and rents may not be raised to cover costs of a condominium or cooperative conversion.
rules.key_value: No state cap; newly constructed multiple dwellings exempt from local rent control for 30 years after completion
rules.coverage_conditions: State notice and unconscionability rules apply to residential rent increases, with any rent caps set by municipal ordinance.
rules.exemptions: Newly constructed multiple dwellings are exempt from local rent control for 30 years after completion of construction, and government-subsidized rents may also be exempt.
rules.quoted_span:
The State of New Jersey has no laws that establish, govern or control rents. Municipalities 
may pass an ordinance establishing rent control or rent leveling.

rules.title: Fair Chance in Housing Act
rules.requirement: Housing providers may not ask about or consider an applicant's criminal record until after a conditional offer. They may never consider non-conviction, expunged, sealed, pardoned, vacated or juvenile records. After an offer, they may consider only listed serious convictions within set look-back periods, and a withdrawal needs an individualized assessment and written notice.
rules.key_value: Post-offer look-back: 6 years for first-degree, 4 years for second/third-degree, 1 year for fourth-degree indictable offenses
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to housing providers renting dwelling units to applicants.
rules.exemptions: Dwelling units in owner-occupied premises of not more than four dwelling units are excluded.
rules.quoted_span:
A housing
provider
shall not make any oral or written inquiry
regarding an applicant’s criminal record prior to making a conditional offer.

rules.title: New Jersey Law Against Discrimination (LAD) – source of lawful income protection
rules.requirement: Landlords may not discriminate in housing based on the source of lawful income or the source of lawful rent or mortgage payment, so they cannot deny a Section 8 voucher holder an apartment solely because of that income source.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to the sale or rental of all property, including open land, for business or residential purposes.
rules.exemptions: Exempts rental of one unit in an owner-occupied two-family dwelling and rental of rooms in an owner-occupied one-family dwelling, among other LAD exceptions.
rules.quoted_span:
The LAD also prohibits housing discrimination  based
on the source of lawful income or source of lawful rent
or mortgage payment a tenant or purchaser uses. This
means, for example, that a landlord cannot deny the
lawful recipient of a Section 8 HUD voucher the right to
rent an apartment based solely on that source of lawful
income.
